1.3:
Consider the following functions I–III of space and time ψ (z,t):

I: ψ (z,t)=exp[-(a²z²+b²t²-2abtz+c)]

II: ψ (z,t)=exp(-c|az-bt|+d)

III: ψ (z,t)=cos(abz +cz²)

a) Under what condition do they propagate at constant velocity and maintain their form? What is the propagation velocity?
b) Under what conditions the perturbations propagate along +z-direction?
c) Which of them are waves? Note that the solutions are evident from the forms of the functions without inserting them into the wave equation. All of the variables and parameters are real. Parameters (a, b, c, d) do not depend on time or position.

EXAMPLE: Function ψ (z,t)=a cos(bcz-dt) is of the familiar time-harmonic plane wave form (retaining its shape) and clearly propagates at constant speed v=(ω)/(k) = (d)/(bc), when a,b,c,d ≠ 0. The perturbation propagates in positive z-direction e.g. when b, c, and d are all positive. The function is a wave since it is twice differentiable with respect to z and t thus fulfilling the wave equation.
1.4:
Consider two harmonic waves Ψⱼ(x, t)=Aⱼ e^(i (k x-ω t+εⱼ)), j=1,2 . Show that their superposition can be expressed in the form Ψₛ(x, t)=ψ₁(x, t)+ψ₂(x, t)=Aₛ e^(i (k x-ω t+εₛ)) and derive the expressions for the amplitude Aₛ and phase εₛ. Hint: Manipulate the superposition into a form that doesn't depend on the phase term φ ≡ kx-ω t. Then with the help of Euler's formula you can calculate the overall phase εₛ using the defining equation θ= atan (Im(z))/(Re(z)) = atan (y)/(x), giving the phase of a complex number z=r e^(i θ). The amplitude Aₛ can be calculated by recalling the geometric meaning of vector addition, and applying the law of cosines. The overall phase and amplitude should be of the familiar form

εₛ =atan((A₁ sin ε₁+A₂ sin ε₂)/(A₁ cos ε₁+A₂ cos ε₂))

Aₛ =√(A₂²+A₁²+2 A₁ A₂ cos (ε₂-ε₁)) .

2.3:
The Lorentz model for an atom can be generalized to include effects in the presence of a static magnetic field B⃗ (such as the Faraday effect) by retaining the Laplace force in the equation of motion for the displacement of an electron x⃗:

m x⃗̈+m γ x⃗̇+k x⃗=q (E⃗(t)+v⃗ × B⃗) ,

where E⃗(t) is a planar and time-harmonic incident electric field and v⃗=x⃗̇. Here, we assume that the static magnetic field points in the z-direction (B⃗=B₀ e⃗_z). We further assume that E⃗(t) is circularly polarized and propagates along z, being therefore of form E⃗(t)=ê_(±)E₀e^(-i ω t), where ê_(±)=(1)/(√(2)) (êₓ ± i ê_(y)).

a) Show via calculation that the identity e⃗_(±) × ê_(z)=± i e⃗_(±) is true.

b) Show that in the above case, the material susceptibility χ becomes

χ_(±)(ω)=(N q²)/(ε₀ m) (1)/(ω₀²-ω² -i γ ω ∓ (q ω)/(m)B₀) ,

in other words, dependent on the handedness of the input polarization. This effect is known as magnetic circular dichroism, and can be used to study properties of many material systems. HINT, use a trial x⃗=x₀ e^(-i ω t)ê_±.
2.4:
One form for the Maxwell's equations is

∇ · D=ρ_(f), ∇ × E=-(∂ B)/(∂ t), ∇ · B=0, ∇ × H=J_(f)+(∂ D)/(∂ t)

where ρ_(f) is the density of free charge, J_(f) is the density of free current, D=ε₀ E+P is the electric displacement and H=B / μ₀-M is the magnetic field, P is the material polarization, and M is the magnetization. Assume the material is charge-neutral dielectric and non-magnetic so that there are no free charges or currents and M=0.

a) Derive generalized wave equations for the fields E and B. They will be of the form

∇ ×(∇ × X)=(factor) (∂² X)/(∂ t²) + (source term due to polarization) ,

Note, that the source term for field E can be different than the source terms for the B-field.

b) Assume an isotropic and homogeneous material so that P=ε₀ χ E (χ is the scalar-valued susceptibility of the material). In this case, the displacement field D⃗ is parallel to the incident field E⃗ and given by D⃗= ε E⃗,
where ε=ε₀(1+ χ) is the material permittivity. Show that in this case the general wave equation for E can be manipulated into the usual wave equation, provided that the speed of light in matter differs from the value in vacuum c₀. Recalling the definition of the refractive index n=c₀/v , express the refractive index as a function of the susceptibility χ.

c) A time-harmonic plane wave E⃗(r⃗,t) = E⃗₀ exp (i n k⃗₀ · r⃗ - ω t) solves the wave equation. How does a non-zero imaginary part of the susceptibility χ qualitatively influence the propagation of a plane wave? Consider both positive and negative imaginary parts (Im (χ) <0 and Im (χ) >0).

3.2:
Scattering from an ensemble of random point-like scatterers. An incident monochromatic, time-harmonic plane wave illuminates an ensemble of N identical, point-like scatterers occupying some finite volume. Each scatterer re-radiates the incident light uniformly into all directions, i.e. it behaves as a point source of a spherical wave (think of the ripples created when you throw a pebble into a lake). The complex electric field scattered by the j-th scatterer (located at rⱼ), evaluated at an observation point P located at r_P, can be written as

Eⱼ(rⱼ,t) = A (exp❴ i k· R ❵)/(‖R‖) exp(i k zⱼ) exp(-iω t) , R ≡ r_P - rⱼ ,

where A is the scattering amplitude, taken to be the same for every scatterer, and k is the wave vector associated with the field at P. The total field at P is obtained by summing the contributions of all N scatterers, E_(T)(r_P,t)=∑ⱼ₌₁^(N)Eⱼ(rⱼ,t).

a) Let P₁=(0,0,z_P) be a point on the optical (z-) axis, located far enough from the scattering volume that ‖r_P‖≈ R₁ can be treated as a constant, independent of j. Derive E_(T) at P₁, and show that the resulting irradiance scales as I_(P₁)∝ N².

b) Let P₂=(x_P,y_P,L) instead be a point located off the z-axis, again far enough away that ‖r_P‖ ≈ R₂ is approximately constant, but now such that the accumulated phase from each scatterer to P₂ does depend on j (and, for a spatially disordered ensemble, varies effectively randomly from scatterer to scatterer). Show that in this case the irradiance instead scales as I_(P₂)∝ N.
3.3:
Let's find out what we can do with simple flat glass slides. Neglect the dispersion of glass and assume it to have a constant refractive index of n = 1.5.

a) Mirror: Somewhat surprisingly, a simple air–glass interface can act as a mirror, when incident at so-called grazing angles. Consider light that is polarized perpendicularly with respect to the plane of incidence. Find out at what incidence angles the interface reflects over 80 % of incident light (R_⊥ > 0.8)? HINT: Calculate and plot a R(θ) curve using, e.g., Matlab.

b) Attenuator: Suppose that we look at a source perpendicularly through a stack of N glass slides, separated from each other by thin air gaps. The source seen through even a dozen slides will be noticeably darker. Assuming negligible absorption, derive the total transmittance of the stack Tₜ as a function of refractive index of the slide n. Evaluate Tₜ for five slides in air. Neglect multiple reflections.

c) Polarizer: Calculate the exact value for the Brewster angle θₚ (when n = 1,5).

d) Waveguide: Explain using a few sentences how a thin glass slide can also act as a waveguide.

4.4:
Fabry–Pérot resonators can also be used as enhancement cavities, allowing to dramatically increase the optical irradiance circulating inside an optical resonator. Provided that incident light is resonant with the cavity (and is mode-matched to its transversal cavity modes), in high-finesse resonators the circulating intracavity power can greatly exceed the incident power. Subsequently, enhancement cavities are used in various applications, where one benefits from high optical power levels.

a) By using the fields and parameters introduced in the figure, derive an enhancement factor for the circulating power inside the enhancement cavity A'_(circ)(φ) ≡ (I_(circ))/(I_(inc)) , where I_(circ) is the irradiance of the circulating field, I_(inc) is the irradiance of the incident field and φ is the phase accumulated during a single round trip inside the cavity (φ = 2kℓ , where k is the amplitude of the wave vector and ℓ is the length of the cavity). Field E_(inc) is incident on the mirror 1 (M₁). Field E_(refl,1) is the field initially reflected at mirror 1, while E_(launch) is the field launched through mirror 1. E_(circ) and E_(b-circ) are the forward and backward circulating fields inside the resonator, respectively. Field E_(RT) corresponds to the field inside the resonator after one round trip and E_(trans) is the field transmitted through mirror 2 (M₂). Interference occurs e.g. at the right-hand side of mirror 1 between E_(launch) and E_(RT), resulting in E_(circ). Mirror reflection (transmission) coefficients are r₁ (t₁) and r₂ (t₂), respectively.

b) Assume that incident light is exactly on resonance with the cavity, i.e. φ = 2 π m, where m is an integer. Show that the enhancement factor can then be written as A'_(circ) = (T₁)/((1- √(R₁ R₂))²)

c) Continue assuming that incident light is exactly on resonance with the cavity. Assume also that the mirror 2 has a reflectivity of R₂ = 99.99 %. What must be the reflectivities of the first mirror R₁ for the power enhancement factor A'_(circ) to reach values of 100, 500, and 1000 (i.e. three values for the reflectivity)?

d) Finally, show that the enhancement factor A'ₜᵣₐₙₛ(φ) ≡ (Iₜᵣₐₙₛ)/(I_(inc)) is of form

A'ₜᵣₐₙₛ(φ) = (1-R₁)(1-R₂) A_(circ)(φ) ,

where A_(circ)(φ) ≡ (I_(circ))/(I_(launch)).

6.4: A convenient way to measure the focal length of a positive lens is by placing a light source a certain distance L from a screen and then placing the lens in between them and finding the two positions at which the lens forms clear images of the source onto the screen. The distance between these two positions is d. It is relatively easy to measure when compared against measuring distances to or from the vertices or the optical center of the lens. What are the limits of focal lengths you can measure with a fixed distance L? Derive the formula for the focal length.
